At that I was wide awake and listening with both ears. Bill laughed. "That was kind of funny, warn't it, Jim?" says he. "You ain't never told me the particulars," says Jim. "Did you have any trouble?" "Well," said Bill. "T'warn't to say easy. That old Jeppard Grimes was a hard old nut. If all Injun fighters was like him, I feel plumb sorry for the Injuns." "If any of them Bear Creek devils ever catches you—" begun Jim. Bill laughed again. "Them hillbillies never strays more'n ten miles from Bear Creek," says he. "I had the sculp and was gone before they knowed what was up. I've collected bounties for wolves and b'ars, but that's the first time I ever got money for a human sculp!" A icy chill run down my spine.

--- Abholos.txt ---

[1] Ghisguth L65
НАЗВАНИЕ: Abholos ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:11:25 СИМВОЛОВ: 810 Abholos Also known as Devourer in the Mist Relatives Tsathoggua (possible brother) Cthulhu (possible parent) Affiliations Great Old Ones First appearance EXP Stunning Eldritch Tales Created by Robin Laws Abholos (also known as Devourer in the Mist ) is a fictional entity created by Robin Laws for the Trail of Cthulhu gaming supplement Stunning Eldritch Tales Overview Abholos is a Great Old One who appears to be a great grey, festering glob of endless malevolence. According to one account, he is a product of Ghisguth and Zstylzhemghi mating, which also gave birth to Tsathoggua . This made Abholos more of a self-willed placenta that had taken form in-and-of-itself, rather than a brother or cousin of the others. According to another account, Abholos is a spawn of Cthulhu , born from his bile and tears.

--- All-Consuming Fire.txt ---

[7] Lloigor L385
P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness Behind the Mythos Elements from the Cthulhu Mythos had previously been incorporated into the Doctor Who universe in the novel White Darkness , by David A. McIntee. However, All-Consuming Fire is notable for identifying several monsters from the original TV series as classic Mythos entities. For instance, the Animus from the serial The Web Planet is implied to be Lloigor , whereas Fenric from the serial The Curse of Fenric is identified as Hastur the Unspeakable , and the Doctor's recurring enemy, the Great Intelligence , is identified as Yog-Sothoth . Additionally, the unnamed Great Old One that the Doctor faced in White Darkness is retroactively identified as Cthulhu . Other entities referred to as Great Old Ones in the novel include Nyarlathotep Dagon , and the Gods of Ragnarok (from The Greatest Show in the Galaxy ).


--- Allan and the Sundered Veil.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L87
Quatermain is taken aback by the two Carters vanishing, but the Time Traveler is not surprised. As he explains to Quatermain, the Time Traveler is the only one whose body is there physically. The others were corporified consciousness, traveling far from where their physical bodies remained, just like Quatermain's body is still in Lady Ragnall's library. When Quatermain also vanishes, the Time Traveler peers into the Aleph and is horrified to see that the adventurer's body has awakened, but is possessed by one of the extracosmic beings. These creatures that are invading reality are identified as the Lloigor , a. k. a. the Great Old Ones . They are the individual components or avatars of an "idea-colony" named Yuggoth : a concept variously identified as a planet, a god, or a state of mind. Despite being aspects of Yuggoth, each Lloigor has its own name and distinct characteristics, as well as an elemental servitor race. The one possessing Quatermain is Ithaqqa , lord of the wind-walkers or Wendigo. Quatermain's disembodied consciousness sees his own body, animated by Ithaqqa, attacking Lady Ragnall and her maid Marisa.

[2] Lloigor L101

Quatermain's disembodied consciousness sees his own body, animated by Ithaqqa, attacking Lady Ragnall and her maid Marisa. He enters his body and fights against the entity. Lady Ragnall dies in shock, but Marisa sees Quatermain's efforts to restrain himself and understands what is happening. She pricks her own hand and uses the blood to draw an ancient talisman while uttering the incantations that she knows can repel the Great Old Ones.

--- Animus.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L15
НАЗВАНИЕ: Animus ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:11:50 СИМВОЛОВ: 1905 Animus Also known as Pwodarauk Lloigor Affiliations Great Old Ones First appearance ADJ : "The Web Planet" Created by Bill Strutton The Animus is an extraterrestrial life form created by the BBC for Doctor Who in 1965. It was later retconned into being a Great Old One during the period when Virgin Books tie-in novels related to Doctor Who were being published in the 1990s. Background The Animus is a Great Old One from the Lloigor race. It was the only one of its race to cross into the physical universe, establishing itself at Vortis and turning the formerly lush planet into an acidic wasteland. It manifested itself within the Carsenome, an organic self-healing palace.

[2] Lloigor L53
НАЗВАНИЕ: Animus ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:11:50 СИМВОЛОВ: 1905 Animus Also known as Pwodarauk Lloigor Affiliations Great Old Ones First appearance ADJ : "The Web Planet" Created by Bill Strutton The Animus is an extraterrestrial life form created by the BBC for Doctor Who in 1965. It was later retconned into being a Great Old One during the period when Virgin Books tie-in novels related to Doctor Who were being published in the 1990s. Background The Animus is a Great Old One from the Lloigor race. It was the only one of its race to cross into the physical universe, establishing itself at Vortis and turning the formerly lush planet into an acidic wasteland. It manifested itself within the Carsenome, an organic self-healing palace. The Animus is capable of taking over anything living which came into contact with gold. It resembled a hybrid created by crossing a spider or plant with an octopus. It could generate a fungus-like sustenance which grew into Carsenome, its fortress.

[1] Lloigor L57
Featuring cover art by Gavin L. O'Keefe and running to 278 pages, it was posthumously published as a paperback by Dancing Tuatara Press and hardback by Ramble House in September 2015. Including an introduction by John Pelan , the collection consists primarily of reprinted stories, with only one, "Spectre over Torsands", being original to this volume. Overview Quite some time before the Lloigor returned, long before anyone had a glimpse of the terrifying Inhabitant of the Lake , and nearly two decades before anyone answered the Caller of the Black or learned what lurked Beneath the Moors, the Call of Cthulhu was first heard in the British Isles by a writer named John S. Glasby. The first British author to transcribe the visions of cosmic horror sent to him in dreams by Great Cthulhu, John S. Glasby produced enough material dealing with the Cthulhu Mythos to fill several collections, of which this is the second to be issued by Dancing Tuatara Press. John Stephen Glasby (1928-2011) started his career as a research chemist for ICI, in 1952 and worked there until his retirement. Always a great fan of the work of H. P.

--- Colin Wilson.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L35
НАЗВАНИЕ: Colin Wilson ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:13:53 СИМВОЛОВ: 2824 Colin Wilson Birth Date June 26, 1931 Birthplace Leicester, Leicestershire, England Death Date December 5, 2013 Deathplace St. Austell, Cornwall, England Nationality British Notable Works The Mind Parasites "The Return of the Lloigor" Spouses Betty Troop, Joy Stewart Colin Wilson (26 June 1931 — 5 December 2013) was an English writer who wrote fiction, including horror and science fiction, works on philosophy, especially philosophy in the Gurdjieff and Existentialist traditions, and nonfiction books on the occult. His novels included Lovecraftian elements, such as cosmic horror and impersonal if hostile entities from outer space. Writing in the 1970s, his works are also more overtly sexual and explicitly violent than those of earlier writers. Wilson's The Strength to Dream: Literature and the Imagination (1962) devoted a chapter to Lovecraft, "that man of dubious genius" who "carried on a lifelong guerrilla warfare against civilisation and materialism."

[2] Lloigor L77
Challenged by August Derleth in the wake of this criticism to show that he could do it better, Wilson produced The Mind Parasites (1967), published by Arkham House , in which humanity is bedeviled by creatures called Tsathogguans . (In a preface, Wilson avers that Lovecraft, "far more than Hemingway or Faulkner, or even Kafka, is a symbol of the outsider-artist in the 20th century".) Wilson then wrote " The Return of the Lloigor ", first published in Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (1969), which turned Derleth's minor Great Old One Lloigor into an alien species of psychic vampires --a depiction that has influenced subsequent writers, including Robert Anton Wilson, Alan Moore , and Grant Morrison Selected Bibliography Fiction The Mind Parasites (1967) The Philosopher's Stone (1969) (Reprinted, Valancourt Books, 2013) The Return of the Lloigor " (first published 1969 in the anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos ; revised separate edition, Village Press, London, 1974). The Space Vampires (1976) Spider World: The Tower (1987) Spider World: The Delta (1987) Spider World: The Magician (1992) The Tomb of the Old Ones (novella published as half of a double volume alongside a novella by John Grant, 2002) Spider World: Shadowland (2002) Nonfiction The Outsider (1956) The Strength to Dream: Literature and the Imagination (1962) (1971) Order of Assassins (1972)


--- Collected Juvenilia.txt ---

[1] Nut L1027
The Tuareg chieftain looked about him with a sneer on his handsome face. With contempt he gazed at the sand dunes. Somehow he felt superior to them. Presently the caravan stopped by an ancient city, half-hidden beneath the sands of the desert. It was almost ruins. A very ancient city; it had been deserted long before Congress began to discuss the immigration problem, even. The Taureg dismounted from his camel and entered his tent. A slave girl offered him a chaw of Beech-nut from her own private plug. He kicked her with a harsh tone of voice. Seating himself on an expensive divan from Bokhara, he reflected meditatively. CHAPTER I "ONE million dollars," mused the Colonel. "Exactly, my dear Colonel," returned Hawkshaw, the great detective, wittily. "But what details of the crime?" "As follows," Hawkshaw replied. "The night watchman of the Stacksuhkale bank, London, was knocked unconscious and a million dollars in American thrift-stamps as well as one million pounds of sterling and a box of fine cigars were taken." "The villain!" exclaimed the Colonel indignantly.

[13] Geb L2097
The sun god as a child on the primeval lotus. In the system of the Heliopolitan ennead five successive gen- erations of deities can be distinguished: the primeval deity Atum creates the first couple Shu and Tefnut, who are not born in the usual way; their offspring Geb, the god of the earth, and Nut, the goddess of the sky, in turn produce four children— Osiris, Seth, Isis, and Nephthys.

[14] Nut L2097
In the New Kingdom and late period the sky goddess Nut, who bore the sun according to the Pyramid Characteristics of the Gods Texts and the moon according to the Coffin Texts,’ often has the epithet "she who bore the gods."

[15] Nut L2101
This epithet refers to the heavenly bodies, whom the sky goddess daily "bears" and again "swallows"—an idea that leads to the depiction of Nut as a sow.

[16] Nut L2101

[1] Cxaxukluth L13
НАЗВАНИЕ: Cthaeghya ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:14:22 СИМВОЛОВ: 3132 Cthaeghya Relatives Cxaxukluth (parent) Cthulhu (brother) Hastur (brother) Ghizguth (brother) Hziulquoigmnzhah (brother) Zstylzhemgni (sister) Klosmiebhyx (sister) Affiliations Great Old Ones First appearance EXP October Surprise Created by Kevin L. O'Brien Cthaeghya is a fictional entity created by Kevin L. O'Brien Cthaeghya is a fictional entity created by Kevin L. O'Brien for his short story " October Surprise ", depicting the character as the sister of Cthulhu and responsible for spawning the Cthulhi Background According to The Book of Merlin , Cthaeghya was birthed by the Outer God known as Cxaxukluth on a black star in the center of a grand nebula, along with her brothers Ghizguth Hzioulquoigmnzhah and Rahb, and their sisters Zstylzhemghi and Klosmiebhyx . Cthaeghya and her family journeyed to Yuggoth , where Rahb mated with the infertile Cthaeghya. They were forced to flee when Cxaxukluth began feeding off its progeny, with Cthaeghya and Rahb fleeing to Xoth . There, Rahb began mating with Idh-yaa , who bore his three sons: Ghatanothoa Ythogtha and Zoth-Ommog . In a fit of rage, Cthaeghya destroyed Idh-yaa and then headed towards Magmhel.

[3] Nug and Yeb L127
A notable case of an entity being well integrated into another author's story-cycle is Smith's Tsathoggua , which Lovecraft mentioned in no less than 10 stories ( one of them unfinished), starting with The Whisperer in Darkness . In his revision of Zealia Bishop The Mound (1940), Lovecraft effectively connected Smith's creation to his story-cycle by placing Tsathoggua alongside such entities as Tulu Yig Shub-Niggurath and Nug and Yeb in subterranean K'n-yan Many of the elements of Lovecraft's Mythos were not a cross-pollination of the various story-cycles of the Lovecraft Circle, but were instead deliberately created by each writer to become part of the Mythos — the most notable example being the various arcane grimoires of forbidden lore. [13] Cxaxukluth L1059
Clark Ashton Smith , in his letters to R. H. Barlow , suggests that Cthulhu is the offspring of the androgynous Cxaxukluth (itself an offspring of Azathoth ), and the brother of Hziulquoigmnzhah and Ghizguth , the latter being the father of Tsathoggua.

In another letter to Barlow, however, Smith names Ptmâk as Cthulhu's "immediate parent" and uses the term "child of Nug".

[15] Nug L1077
It is not clear whether Smith intended the "child of Nug" to be Ptmâk or Cthulhu.

--- Cthulhu_Files_Store_a091568afc [Cthulhu Files Store_9.txt].txt ---

[1] Yeb L23
H. Barlow Lovecraft's young protegé and literary executor, Barlow was responsible for preserving Lovecraft's manuscripts. He later became a distinguished professor of anthropology. Eyes of the God: Selected Writings of R. H. Barlow (Second Edition, Revised and Expanded) Collects Barlow's early fantasy stories, some written in collaboration with Lovecraft, including many that were long available only in the pages of fan publications from the 1930s. Included is a brief series, "The Annals of the Jinn" that is in the vein of Lovecraft's dreamlands series and Smith's Hyperborean fantasies. There are passing references to some Lovecraftian entities such as Nyarlathotep, Azathoth, Shub-Niggurath, and Yeb, as well as the Smithian Tsathoggua (here called Zotog-Ua). The volume also includes Barlow's poetry and a selection of his nonfiction, including moving essays about Lovecraft and Henry S. Whitehead. The greatly expanded second edition runs to 596 pages. Marcos Legaria, L'Affaire Barlow Bringing Lovecraft's works to a mainstream audience was a journey fraught with complications. In L’Affaire Barlow, the author shows how dangerously close Lovecraft’s work was to being litigated into obscurity. Bruised egos, personal vendettas, and Machiavellian plots abound, making control of the Lovecraft literary estate read like a tale from one of the pulp magazines.


--- Cthulhu_Mythos_The_H.P._Lovecraft_Wiki_Fandom_84a4d920e1.txt ---

[3] Nug and Yeb L261
A notable case of an entity being well integrated into another author's story-cycle is Smith's Tsathoggua, which Lovecraft mentioned in no less than 10 stories (one of them unfinished), starting with The Whisperer in Darkness. In his revision of Zealia Bishop's The Mound (1940), Lovecraft effectively connected Smith's creation to his story-cycle by placing Tsathoggua alongside such entities as Tulu, Yig, Shub-Niggurath and Nug and Yeb in subterranean K'n-yan.

[9] Zhar and Lloigor L375
Finally, Derleth matched the earth beings against the fire beings, and the air beings against the water beings, which is not consistent with the traditional elemental dichotomy (namely, that air opposes earth and fire opposes water). The Elemental Classifications[] Derleth's Elemental Classifications Air Earth Fire Water Hastur Ithaqua* Zhar and Lloigor* Nyarlathotep Shub-Niggurath Tsathoggua Yog-Sothoth Cthugha* Cthulhu * a deity created by Derleth Lin Carter's Elemental Classifications Air Earth Fire Water Hastur Ithaqua Rhan-Tegoth Zhar and Lloigor Nyarlathotep Nyogtha Shub-Niggurath Tsathoggua Aphoom-Zhah* Cthugha Cthulhu Dagon Ghatanothoa Mother Hydra Ythogtha* Zoth-Ommog* * a deity created by Carter Conclusion[] Derleth became a publisher of Lovecraft's stories after his death. Lovecraft himself was very critical of his own writings and was often easily discouraged, especially when faced with any rejection of his work. If it were not for Derleth, Lovecraft's writings and the Cthulhu Mythos would have remained largely unknown.

--- Dr. Fo-Lan.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L89
Fo-Lan is incredibly knowledgeable in the matters of the Cthulhu Mythos and has even mastered the art of astral projection, although he refers to it as "telepathy". At the end of the nineteenth century, Fo-Lan was abducted from his home in Peiping by the Tcho-Tcho people , who brought him to their hidden city of Alaozar, in the Burmese Plateau of Sung . Fo-Lan's brother was killed, presumably disfigured to prevent identification, and left in Fo-Lan's place, leading the world to believe that the doctor himself had been murdered. For the next three years, the captive Fo-Lan reluctantly helped the Tcho-Tchos and their leader E-poh to dig deeper into the heart of the Plateau, until they found the chamber where Lloigor was imprisoned. Unbeknownst to his captors, Fo-Lan spent all his spare time trying to use astral projection to contact the Elder Gods in the Orion Belt. When the Tcho-Tchos captured an American explorer named Eric Marsh and brought him to Alaozar, Fo-Lan convinced them to spare the man's life by claiming that Marsh could help them.

[2] Zhar and Lloigor L97
For the next three years, the captive Fo-Lan reluctantly helped the Tcho-Tchos and their leader E-poh to dig deeper into the heart of the Plateau, until they found the chamber where Lloigor was imprisoned. Unbeknownst to his captors, Fo-Lan spent all his spare time trying to use astral projection to contact the Elder Gods in the Orion Belt. When the Tcho-Tchos captured an American explorer named Eric Marsh and brought him to Alaozar, Fo-Lan convinced them to spare the man's life by claiming that Marsh could help them. Fo-Lan told Marsh the story of how the Elder Gods imprisoned Zhar and Lloigor Star-Warriors of Orion descended from the stars to destroy the twin monstrosities and their servants, followed later by the Elder Gods themselves, one of which transported Fo-Lan and Marsh to safety. A Tokyo newspaper later published the news about Fo-Lan being still alive. By the time Eric Marsh wrote his narrative, he told readers that they could seek out Fo-Lan in the village of Bangka, in the province of Shan-si, if they wanted to confirm the veracity of the events narrated. ( AWD The Lair of the Star-Spawn

--- Elder God.txt ---

[1] Zhar and Lloigor L81
These gigantic beings from outer space descended swiftly, circling the Plateau of Sung , and from them great rays of stabbing light shot out toward the hidden fastnesses below. And at the same time, the earth began to tremble. Eric Marsh ( AWD The Lair of the Star-Spawn The Elder Gods , also referred to as the Elder Deities , are fictional extraterrestrial entities featured in the Cthulhu Mythos . They are originally described as looking like huge pillars of light or fire, which dwell in the vicinity of the star Betelgeuse , and are known to protect humans while being inimical to the "evil" gods such as Cthulhu Hastur Zhar and Lloigor AWD The Lair of the Star-Spawn The Horror from the Depths "). In the Expanded Mythos, they originate from another dimension, have mostly human-like appearance and are benevolent in nature. In different parts of the world - such as Egypt, Mesoamerica, and the Mediterranean - they were worshipped by ancient humans. Nowadays, they are remembered as the gods in just about every ancient race, including Greek, Norse, Egyptian, Aztec, and many others.

--- Eric Marsh.txt ---

[1] Zhar and Lloigor L83
( AWD The Lair of the Star-Spawn Eric Marsh was an explorer and aide de camp to the explorer Hawks. He was with Hawks when the latter along with the rest of his expedition were slaughtered by the Tcho-Tcho. Marsh survived in an injured condition and eventually through his own offers of violence and heroic efforts escaped captivity and made his way back to civilization. The events however gave him permanent phobias and left his expanded mind, already affected by exposure to the entities Zhar and Lloigor , permanently damaged.

--- Fomalhaut.txt ---

[1] Zhar and Lloigor L23
НАЗВАНИЕ: Fomalhaut ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:18:14 СИМВОЛОВ: 1707 Fomalhaut Also known as Alpha Piscis Austrini Alpha PsA α Piscis Austrini α PsA Ruling Powers Zhar and Lloigor Inhabitants Tcho-Tcho People (possibly) First appearance AWD The Trail of Cthulhu Fomalhaut is the brightest star in the constellation Piscis Austrinus and one of the brightest stars in the sky. It is a class A star on the main sequence approximately 25 light-years (7.7 pc) from Earth as measured by the Hipparcos astrometry satellite. Since 1943, the spectrum of this star has served as one of the stable anchor points by which other stars are classified. It is classified as a Vega-like star that emits excess infrared radiation, indicating it is surrounded by a circumstellar disk. Fomalhaut, K-type star TW Piscis Austrini and M-type star LP 876-10 constitute a triple system even though the companions are separated by several degrees.


--- From the Parchments of Pnom.txt ---

[1] Cxaxukluth L101
His main source, albeit not the only one, is an ancient text called the Parchments of Pnom . The time period is unknown, although the scholar mentions a type of whiskey that is "imported from Mars He starts out by revealing that, while Azathoth's androgynous children reproduced asexually like their parent, many of their offspring were single-gendered. For instance, the androgynous Cxaxukluth spawned at least two male sons: Hziulquoigmnzhah and Ghizguth , the latter which married Zstylzhemgni and fathered Tsathoggua. He also mentions a descendant of the gods named Knygathin Zhaum , who regained the Azathothian ability to spawn amorphous children after " the stress of his numerous decapitations ", and hints of another legend that he hasn't translated yet. For details concerning a deity named Tulu or Cthulhu , the author recommends that the correspondent contact a certain Ech-Pi-El , who can provide more information.

[2] Cxaxukluth L137
He also mentions a descendant of the gods named Knygathin Zhaum , who regained the Azathothian ability to spawn amorphous children after " the stress of his numerous decapitations ", and hints of another legend that he hasn't translated yet. To escape his parent's cannibalistic inclinations, Hziulquoigmnzhah moved on to Yaksh , where the natives worshiped him, then onto Cykranosh , followed aeons later by his nephew Tsathoggua. The encounter of Eibon with Hzioulquoigmnzhah many ages later is mentioned.

--- GAMING_SCENARIO_2c44daa60b.txt ---

[1] Nut L51
Keeping the adventure closer to home and more commonplace makes it a lot more terrifying. (Saving the world scenarios never did much for me.) Priceless fits in as a tool. He will continue to paint clues he receives via dreams. Each dream helps zero him in on locations, landmarks, etc. In fact, Priceless wouldn't really care if there wasn't such a drawback. Every new dream-inspired painting saps him of one point of strength and 4 sanity points; enough to keep him weak and right on edge without totally losing it. Receiving a dream once a week is a slow burn, enough to keep him out of the nut house. However, soon enough, it could kill him. Next Steps: The rest of the scenario depends on a clever Keeper. There is a lot of room for improvisation, and working in things from a larger campaign. This scenario can take either a few hours or a few sessions, depending on your likes and dislikes. What's Happening: Over the next four weeks a new dream will be received by Priceless and his health and sanity will deteriorate.

--- Gnoph-keh.txt ---

[1] Zhar L77
P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald For the human Hyperborea species, see Gnophkeh Gnoph-keh , also known as Gnoph-Hek are sharp-horned, coarse-haired beings with six long-limbs, found in Greenland and the Arctic Circle. Empowered with blizzard summoning and reducing temperatures. Connected with Rhan-Tegoth (whom they seem to worship) and possibly Ithaqua Zhar and Lloigor (god). In early texts (such as the Book of Eibon ) it is a race of vicious cannibals who were driven from Lomar by mankind and the Voormis , but in later texts it appears as a lone creature, sometimes called "the Hairy Thing" and is confused with Rhan-Tegoth. Some texts call them "reptilian" although hairy reptiles are far from common. It is now on the brink of extinction and only encountered in ones. The Gnophkeh are either creatures of air or water.


--- Gods and Myths of Northern Europe (H.R. Ellis Davidson) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).txt ---

[9] Nut L2741
Accordingly he borrowed the falcon shape of Freyja and flew off to Thiazi’s abode. The giant was out fishing, so Loki changed Idun into a nut and flew off with it in his claws. Thiazi discovered the loss and started in pursuit, and Loki flew into Asgard only just in time.

[14] Nut L6313
Apples and nuts from the land of promise, renewing youth and freeing those who ate them from the tyranny of time, are a familiar feature in Irish sagas, and one that goes back to an early date. It may be noted that on one occasion Loki turned Idun and her apples into a nut, and escaped with it in his claws as he flew in the form of a bird (see p. 39 ). Here then we have the association between eternal youth and nuts and apples which is found in the Irish stories. Conceivably however the association of fruit, and particularly the apple, with the gods was already present in Germanic heathenism.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Great Old Ones Can Be Summoned (August Derleth's Cthulhu Mythos) ИСТОЧНИК: Great Old Ones Can Be Summoned Though the Great Old Ones (3) are said to be imprisoned, there are many instances of them appearing on Earth in recent times. For example, there have been visits in modern times from Hastur Hastur Cthulhu Hastur Island Lloigor Sandwin Ithaqua Beyond2 Ithaqua Wind Nyarlathotep Dweller Yog-Sothoth Lurker Derleth never explains this paradox. However, it seems that the Great Old Ones (3) can be summoned temporarily by their devotees: They walk unseen, They walk foul in lonely places where the Words have been spoken and the Rites howled through at Their Seasons, which are in the blood and differ from the seasons of man. [ Lurker ][paraphrased from HPL Dunwich online text )] These temporary visits are evidently not the full escape that the Great Old Ones (3) crave.

--- Greek Religion (Walter Burkert) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).txt ---

[9] Seb L12775
Yet in the later language this word has fallen into disuse, while the word newly formed from the same root, deisidaimon fearing daimons, is used almost exclusively in a pejorative sense to mean superstition, that which seems ridiculous. Have the Greeks ‘forgotten the experience of the creeps’? To designate the awe that spreads from the gods the root seb- appears; etymologically it too points back to danger and flight, yet in Greek, reverence and admiration come to the fore: ‘ sebas holds me as I behold’; a moderate mysterium tremendum is transferred into augustum. Sebesthai is close to aideisthai and almost coincides with hazesthai . Gods and everything that belongs to them, festivals, temples, sacrifices, are semna , revered, grand, and august, and so too are clothes, manner of speech, and behaviour at the festivals of the gods.

[9] Nug L343
From the whole mass of gold and stone a monotonous roar of activity droned outward over the plain, while cavalcades and streams of wagons were constantly entering and leaving over the great gold- or stone-paved roads. Several times Gll’-Hthaa-Ynn paused to shew Zamacona some particular object of interest, especially the temples of Yig, Tulu, Nug, Yeb, and the Not-to-Be-Named One which lined the road at infrequent intervals, each in its embowering grove according to the custom of K’n-yan. [10] Nug and Yeb L343
These temples, unlike those of the deserted plain beyond the mountains, were still in active use; large parties of mounted worshippers coming and going in constant streams. Gll’-Hthaa-Ynn took Zamacona into each of them, and the Spaniard watched the subtle orgiastic rites with fascination and repulsion. The ceremonies of Nug and Yeb sickened him especially—so much, indeed, that he refrained from describing them in his manuscript. One squat, black temple of Tsathoggua was encountered, but it had been turned into a shrine of Shub-Niggurath, the All-Mother and wife of the Not-to-Be-Named One. This deity was a kind of sophisticated Astarte, and her worship struck the pious Catholic as supremely obnoxious.

--- Hugh B. Cave, The Death Watch [The Death Watch by Hugh B. Cave.txt].txt ---

[1] Nut L385
He pulled open a drawer. There were more books in the drawer—books of a different sort. "Some of these were in the house when we came here," he said. "Mark must have been studying them. Others I obtained by mail, from a collector." I skimmed through a couple of them, but it was all Greek to me. Stuff about the Black Mass and Bethmoora and the black lakes of Hali. Stuff about voodoo and the dark arts. "Hell," I said, "only a nut would bother wading through this junk. What’s eating you, anyway?" "She reads it," he said. "Who? Elaine?" "Yes." "You mean she takes this junk seriously?" He nodded. I didn’t like the way he stared at me, or the way he handled those books when he replaced them in the drawer. He seemed to resent my disbelief, and he touched the books the way some folks touch a Bible. Reverently, sort of. Then suddenly he said: "Elaine mustn’t know about this. You understand? She thinks I’m working on a novel." "That’s what I thought, too," I said.


--- Hyperborea.txt ---

[1] Nug and Yeb L165
It is in fact an interdimensional hub connected to multiple worlds, and indirectly connected with the Cavern of Archetypes. Atlach-Nacha originated here. Cavern of Archetypes The cavern of the Archetypes is a vast cavern inhabited by the spectral archetypes of all life on this earth. Nug and Yeb reside here. Commoriom Commoriom was the first seat of power in Hyperborea, established by the pre-human migrants from the south. In its heyday, Commoriom was a grand city, built of marble and granite and marked by a skyline of altitudinous spires. Legend has it that the populace fled Commoriom when the White Sybil of Polarion foretold of its destruction.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Independent race ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:21:38 СИМВОЛОВ: 1945 Independent races are one of the three categories employed to classify species in the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu , along with servitor races and fabulous creatures . Unlike servitor races, independent races are not intrinsically associated with one particular deity . While some might be irreligious, others might still form cults. The game further classifies them as "Greater Independent Races" or "Lesser Independent Races", depending on the danger posed by an average individual of the species. The titular creature debuted in August Derleth 's short story " The Thing That Walked on the Wind ", which was inspired by Algernon Blackwood 's 1910 tale The Wendigo Background Ithaqua is one of the Great Old Ones Wendigo and possibly the Yeti Ithaqua's cult is small, but he is greatly feared in the far north. Fearful denizens of Siberia, Canada , and Alaska often leave sacrifices for Ithaqua; not as worship but as appeasement. Those who join his cult are granted immunity to extremely cold temperatures.

[2] Zhar and Lloigor L157
The titular creature debuted in August Derleth 's short story " The Thing That Walked on the Wind ", which was inspired by Algernon Blackwood 's 1910 tale The Wendigo Background Ithaqua is one of the Great Old Ones Wendigo and possibly the Yeti Ithaqua's cult is small, but he is greatly feared in the far north. However, in at least one of the many conflicts among the Great Old Ones, Ithaqua seems to have sided with Cthulhu against Hastur and Cthugha AWD The Black Island Friedrich von Junzt Unaussprechlichen Kulten claims that Ithaqua, Zhar, and Lloigor are the children of Hastur and Shub-Niggurath EXP The Horror in the Gallery Ithaqua might be the same entity as Avaloth , and possibly Aphoom-Zhah EXP Wrath of the Wind-Walker "), although the latter is generally regarded as a child of Cthugha ( EXP The Acolyte of the Flame Ithaqua figures prominently in Brian Lumley Titus Crow Mythos series, ruling the ice-world of Borea. In Lumley's works, Ithaqua periodically treads the winds of space between Earth and Borea, bringing helpless victims back to Borea to worship him among its snowy wastes. He frequently attempts to reproduce with humanoid females, hoping to create offspring which can surpass his own limitations, imposed by the Elder Gods , and so help free the rest of the Great Old Ones. It is suggested that Ithaqua has the ulterior motive of desiring offspring to assuage his bitter loneliness, as he is the only one of his kind.


--- Ithaqua_(Cthulhu_Universalis)_08abd65f96 [Ithaqua (Cthulhu Universalis).txt].txt ---

[1] Lloigor L43
Presumably his movements are limited in some way, or perhaps he can manifest only for short periods of time. Air Elementals Ithaqua is said to be a creature of the air, and an elemental force of evil. Ithaqua is the god of the winds , ruler of the air , and rides the winds high above earth. Marius Phillips thought Ithaqua was a "representation" of the elemental force of air. Ithaqua belongs to a subgroup of the Ancient Ones (2) who are air elementals; these also include Lloigor, Zhar, and Hastur. They walk the winds and interstellar space. Names Laban Shrewsbury saw parallels between Ithaqua and the Wendigo of the northwoods Indians. Shrewsbury said that Ithaqua, ruler of the air, is akin to the fabled Wendigo. Josiah Alwyn said that certain of the Indians refer to Ithaqua as the Wendigo. On the other hand, Marius Phillips thought that Ithaqua was a "cousin" of the Wendigo. The term "Wind-Walker" is sometimes regarded as another name for Ithaqua.

[2] Lloigor L65
They walk the winds and interstellar space. Names Laban Shrewsbury saw parallels between Ithaqua and the Wendigo of the northwoods Indians. Shrewsbury said that Ithaqua, ruler of the air, is akin to the fabled Wendigo. Josiah Alwyn said that certain of the Indians refer to Ithaqua as the Wendigo. On the other hand, Marius Phillips thought that Ithaqua was a "cousin" of the Wendigo. The term "Wind-Walker" is sometimes regarded as another name for Ithaqua. However, Jonathan Bishop that the "Walker on ye Wind" is known by several names, namely Windeego (Wendigo), Ithaka (Ithaqua), or Loegar (Lloigor). Thus, he seemed to believe that these are all different names for a single entity. Ithaqua is also known as Death-Walker, Ithaka, Lord of the Winds, and Snow-Thing. Leaders, Rivals, and Allies David, a librarian at Miskatonic, said that Hastur, Ithaqua, and Lloigor lead the forces of air. But Ithaqua seems a lesser being than Hastur: for Henry Lucas prayed for Ithaqua to take his body to the feet of that greater being, Hastur.

[3] Lloigor L81
Leaders, Rivals, and Allies David, a librarian at Miskatonic, said that Hastur, Ithaqua, and Lloigor lead the forces of air. But Ithaqua seems a lesser being than Hastur: for Henry Lucas prayed for Ithaqua to take his body to the feet of that greater being, Hastur. There is a feud between Hastur and Cthugha on the one hand, and Cthulhu and Ithaqua on the other. Some of the Ancient Ones have devotees in common with Ithaqua. The beings at Sandwin house chanted to Ithaqua along with Lloigor, Shub-Niggurath, and Cthulhu ; and the voices outside Josiah Alwyn's house chanted to Ithaqua along with Cthulhu and Shub-Niggurath. Voices heard in the Wood of N'gai indicated that Ithaqua shall serve the "Father of the million favored ones"; that is, Nyarlathotep. The Great Race fled to the future to escape Ithaqua ("That which Walketh on ye Winds") and the Elder Things (1) ("ye winds & ye Voices"), and will do so again. From this, it appears that the Elder Things are allies or servants of Ithaqua.

[4] Lloigor L169
However, Lucas spoke as if it were a punishment he had incurred. One of Ithaqua's traveling companions was apparently not a victim. Asa Sandwin said that he had ridden with Ithaqua high over the face of the earth, over Egypt and Samarkand, Hawaii and the Pacific, and the great white silences. Sandwin said that he was not afraid of Ithaqua, and could foil him. Eventually Sandwin fell victim to a different air elemental, Lloigor. Appearance Ithaqua is the one god of whom no totems bear sign. However, Josiah Alwyn's body was found with a stone miniature of a monstrosity walking on the winds above the earth. At night, Ithaqua may appear simply as a huge dark outline against the stars, a horrible caricature of man. He is similarly described as a giant man-shaped shadow with two starlike eyes.


--- K'n-yanian.txt ---

[1] Nug and Yeb L105
Similarly the society and culture of the K'n-yanians has collapsed into barbaric splendor, with bloodsport and other similar entertainments replacing their previous intellectual pursuits. The natives of K'n-yan are immortal (except by violence or suicide), and have fallen into decline by losing interest in having all their needs met. To survive the boredom, they indulged in grotesque entertainments and the worship of sinister gods they had discovered while exploring the abyss of N'kai (where they had encounters with the Formless Spawn of Tsathoggua ). The natives worshiped Azathoth Nyarlathotep Ghatanothoa Nug and Yeb and Shub-Niggurath , as well as Han the Dark. Their titular gods, to whom they dedicate rich shrines and statues, are Yig and Cthulhu , whom they call "Tulu." According to them, Tulu brought with him an alien metal, which they use as currency after they extracted it from ancient cyclopean idols created on other worlds. This metal was shown to be the only substance that could harm or ward off the K'n-Yanians while they were intangible. Tulu also taught them to write in the R'lyeh glyph form, which has evolved over time.

--- Kishin Houkou Demonbane (OVA).txt ---

[1] Zhar and Lloigor L57
It was accompanied with the limited DX and KADOKAWA THE Best version of the eponymous visual novel , taking place at some point during the main story. Synopsis After arriving in Arkham City, aspiring photojournalist Lilli M. Bridge got a job at the Daily Arkham, a newspaper publisher that was looking for pictures of the giant robot Demonbane to include in their articles. Lilli tries to interview several of the residents including Leica Crusade, Lieutenant Stone and Daijuuji Kurou, but has little to no success at getting any information. When she encounters Al Azif in an area that was restricted by the Hadou Financial Group, Lilli discovers a mysterious piece of alloy as well as successfully photographing Al's missing fragments, known as Zhar and Lloigor . Lilli was nearly attacked by the fragments before being rescued by Kurou. Back at the Daily Arkham, Lilli's boss had no interest in Zhar and Lloigor, referring to it as an "insignificant occult incident" and scolds her for not getting photos of Demonbane instead. However, the alloy that she retrieved was speculated to be created by the Hadou Financial Group, leading to Lilli coming to the conclusion that the organization must have some connection to Demonbane.

--- Knygathin Zhaum.txt ---

[1] Cxaxukluth L109
The child of Sfatlicllp and a Voormi , Knygathin Zhaum was a reaver and cannibal. Upon its capture by the constabulary of Commoriom , headsman Athammaus attempted to execute it by beheading, but because of its preternatural heritage, such attempts proved unsuccessful and only served to temporarily inconvenience the creature. As the folks of Commoriom realised that they stood no chance against this seemingly-unkillable entity, they left the fabulous city to its fate and re-established the capital at Uzuldaroum. As a descendant of Cxaxukluth , Knygathin Zhaum reproduced by fission and thus created an Azathothian strain among the Hyperborean Voormi, with which it later repopulated Hyperborea after humankind deserted the capital city of Commoriom.

For the Great Old One see Zhar and Lloigor The Lloigor (also known as The Invisible Ones from the Stars ) are a fictional species from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos . They first appeared in the short story " The Return of the Lloigor " by Colin Wilson Description The Lloigor are vortices of living power completely invisible except on occasions when they appear reptilian. They came from Andromeda, first settling in Lemuria and Mu . They used humans as slaves (see the Kthatans), have the power to transform people physically and can adopt corporal bodies if they wish. They are sometimes called "the invisible ones from the stars" and may be the same as the flying polyps . They were ruled by Ghatanothoa possibly through mating with the god Lloigor

--- Many-Angled One.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L15
НАЗВАНИЕ: Many-Angled One ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:24:20 СИМВОЛОВ: 4382 Many-Angled One Sociocultural Characteristics Also known as Lloigor Old Ones Elder Gods Chthonic Deities Chthonic Entities Nameless Ones Undying Ones Great Old Ones Outsiders Origin Unknown Real World Information First appearance ADJ 2000 AD Vol 1 536 Appearances EXP The Thanos Imperative The Laundry Files Created by Grant Morrison The Many-Angled Ones are a race of extradimensional entities from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos . The term "Many-Angled One" was originally created by Grant Morrison for Zenith , a series published in the science fiction comic magazine 2000 AD by Fleetway Publications. It would later be used for several other works, most notably in Marvel Comics Zenith The Many-Angled Ones (also known as the Lloigor ) exist in a space that contains more dimensions than our universe therefore they appear to humans as "many angled."

[2] Lloigor L87
The term "Many-Angled One" was originally created by Grant Morrison for Zenith , a series published in the science fiction comic magazine 2000 AD by Fleetway Publications. It would later be used for several other works, most notably in Marvel Comics Zenith The Many-Angled Ones (also known as the Lloigor ) exist in a space that contains more dimensions than our universe therefore they appear to humans as "many angled." Therefore when one of them manifests in our universe, it appears to us as the floating disconnected body parts of a larger creature. Unlike most Lovecraftian entities, that often seem to have unknown albeit hostile motivations, the goal of the Many-Angled Ones is to impose on the multiverse a rigid geometrical order thereby making everything run like clockwork. No matter what host body a Many-Angled One takes, it possesses superhuman strength, reflexes, and speed. It's extremely durable and nearly invulnerable. From the eyes it incredibly destructive beams.

[1] Nug and Yeb L79
They were based on the pseudoscientific writings of Augustus Le Plongeon and James Churchward , who equated Mu with Atlantis and Lemuria , respectively. In the Cthulhu Mythos , these three continents are portrayed as distinct nations that coexisted and traded with each other during the same precataclysmic time period ( CIRCLE The Shadow Kingdom HPL Bothon CIRCLE The Warder of Knowledge The Muvians were first incorporated into the Mythos by Hazel Heald and H. P. Lovecraft in their short story " Out of the Aeons In the Mythos Religion The people of Mu worshiped many different deities , including Ghatanothoa Shub-Niggurath Yig Nug and Yeb HPL Out of the Aeons Cthulhu Iod Vorvadoss CIRCLE The Invaders "), and Ythogtha K'naa EXP The Thing in the Pit Every year, the priests of Ghatanothoa sacrificed 12 young warriors and 12 young maidens to their god on the flaming altars of a marble temple at the base of Mt. Yaddith-Gho . The people of Mu believed that, without these sacrifices to appease it, Ghatanothoa would emerge from the mountain and cast its petrifying gaze on all below.

[4] Lloigor L297
This happened about 1,800 years before the time of General Bothon ( HPL Bothon "). Therefore, if one assumes that the disaster witnessed by Bothon was the same witnessed by Zanthu, which has been attributed to Ythogtha ( EXP The Thing in the Pit "), the Muvian colonisation of Atlantis might possibly be dated to circa 163,644 BC. During the Thurian Age, the kingdom of Valusia employed mercenaries from Mu and Kaa-u. The Lloigor treated the Muvians with utmost brutality, not only enslaving them, but punishing any act of rebelliousness by amputating their limbs or causing cancerous tentacles to grow out of their eyes or other parts of their bodies. When it first started, I was a little dubious about whether it would capture my interest. But, indeed, it succeeded. Sunday - Day 3 The Cthulhu Prayer Breakfast. If you didn't attend the breakfast, you really have to attend the next one. I know the price was a little steep for a breakfast, but what occurred therein more than made up for it. After Bob Price gave his invocation and got Joe Pulver to assist with the "Litany to Nug and Yeb" from the Book of Eibon, the guests of honor got to speak: Fred Chappell, Jason Eckhardt, and W. Panel: Lovecraft's Poetry, with Fred Chappell, S. T. Joshi, and Darrell Schweitzer. Not a great fan of poetry by any standard, this panel was interesting from the standpoint of hearing HPL's poetry read. I can't remember which poem Fred read, but I believe it was one of the Fungi.

[2] Lloigor L545
This translation is rife with inaccuracies and fanciful ideas that were added by the author. It contains such outlandish misconceptions as Cthulhu being a manifestation of Nyarlathotep , and Abhoth having created the Solar System. Although this "translation" is commonly called the Sussex Manuscript , its proper title is Cultus Maleficarum Das Verichteraraberbuch Friedrich von Junzt made a translation into German from an unknown Greek copy. This translation was published in Ingolstadt eight years after his death in 1840, but there are few further details. ( EXP : The "Schrödinger's Cat Trilogy", Robert Anton Wilson) The Voynich manuscript A secret encrypted Arabian copy of the Necronomicon EXP : "Return of the Lloigor", Colin Wilson This version is inspired by the real life Voynich manuscript, a text likely dating from the 1400s whose exact nature has been a cause for much debate. The Book of the Ancient Demons In 1512, León de Sagredo, of Tárrega, translated a copy of the Necronomicon found in Salamanca into Spanish as El Libro De Los Antiguos Demonios Escrito por el Arabe Abdul Hazred . It was based on an Arabic copy, potentially the original, found by the physician Avendath in 1164.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Nug-Soth (alphabet) ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:26:32 СИМВОЛОВ: 1998 Nug-Soth Created by Abdul Alhazred Place of origin Middle East Type Alphabet Function Communications tool Real World Information Creator George Hay Colin Wilson First Appearance EXP : "Ye Alphabet of Nug-Soth" In Colin Wilson 's work on the Necronomicon , "Ye Alphabet of Nug-Soth" is the name of an alphabet that was created as some kind of esoteric scripture, to serve the purpose of the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred for his great work, the Necronomicon . It is also used on talismans to help its user to travel through time and space.

[2] Nug L59
It is also used on talismans to help its user to travel through time and space. The alphabet might have been inspired by the "runes of Nug-Soth" mentioned in Fritz Leiber 's 1976 story " The Terror from the Depths Behind the Mythos In the Necronomicon by George Hay and Colin Wilson , published 1978, various Lovecraft works and names from those works and the broader Cthulhu Mythos are namechecked but recontextualized, as with the use of the name of an alien race, the Nug-Soth , for an alphabet, without any direct connection to imply that this might be the alphabet used by that alien species. One can infer such a thing, but such a statement or inference is not present in the 1978 work. In this sense, Wilson and Hay are really using Mythos names as labels for disparate and in many cases arguably unrelated material.

[3] Nug L91
One can infer such a thing, but such a statement or inference is not present in the 1978 work. In this sense, Wilson and Hay are really using Mythos names as labels for disparate and in many cases arguably unrelated material. The Nug-Soth letters are based on the Coelbren inscriptions in Coelbren, Glamorganshire, Wales , and on the allegedly forged alphabet alleged to have been created rather than discovered by Iolo Morganwg, and first described by Iolo Morganwg's son Taliesin ab Iolo in works published in 1840. The Dark Age inscriptions from the sixth century AD and earlier are matters of historical fact. Using the Coelbren Script, in the form in which it appears on the Dark Age stonework and graves rather than the simplified form from Morganwg, implies several interesting links to the historical King Arthur, ley lines and the Lloigor and was undoubtedly intended to do so given the bent of Wilson's other contributions to the Mythos.

--- Once Men.txt ---

[1] Nug L101
As the story recounts, Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee ’s mind is exchanged with that of one of the Great Race of Yith . While his mind is in the distant past, he encounters other human minds from various epochs. Among these are three men from the future. The first is Nevil Kingston-Brown, an " Australian physicist... who will die in 2,518 A. D." The second is Yiang-Li who is "a philosopher from the cruel empire of Tsan-Chan , which is to come in 5,000 A. D." The third is Nug-Soth , "a magician of the dark conquerors of 16,000 A. D." The story also relates that a hardy coleopterous race will be humanity’s immediate successor on earth . Unfortunately for that race of beetles, they will eventually be taken over by the minds of the Great Race. The final race on earth, at least according to the story, will be an arachnid one. While no specific dates are provided, these events lie in the distant future.

--- Plateau of Sung.txt ---

НАЗВАНИЕ: Plateau of Sung ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:27:03 СИМВОЛОВ: 624 Not to be confused with the Plateau of Tsang Plateau of Sung Location Burma First appearance AWD The Lair of the Star-Spawn Created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer The Plateau of Sung is a plateau in Burma on which the Tcho-Tcho People are centered. The city of Alaozar stood on the Isle of Stars in the Lake of Dread, hidden from common view by a barrier of trees (if they were trees). The gods Lloigor and Zhar are situated here. Sometimes called the Sung Region, the area is shunned by the non-Tcho-Tcho natives, and few men have penetrated the jungles to approach it. It is sometimes confused with the Plateau of Leng

--- Red Star, Yellow Sign.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L57
It was published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in April 2011. Synopsis In the aftermath of the unexplained assassination of a senior Soviet politician, man named Yezhov is tasked with uncovering the motive for this attack on the State. He soon uncovers a plot by mystical forces to interfere in the affairs of humankind and, after discovering the entity controlling the human assassin - a monstrous Lloigor - embarks on a course of action which he believes will result in the purging of all supernatural elements from his country. The story is interspersed with a series of missives between R'lyeh and the Leningrad Operational Center. These reveal that the initial assassination attempt was the result of poorly-planned meddling in human affairs; the final one explains how the manipulation of Yezhov and the sacrifice of a Lloigor agent had resulted in a violent program which would keep the secrets of the supernatural puppet masters safe for centuries.

[2] Lloigor L65
He soon uncovers a plot by mystical forces to interfere in the affairs of humankind and, after discovering the entity controlling the human assassin - a monstrous Lloigor - embarks on a course of action which he believes will result in the purging of all supernatural elements from his country. The story is interspersed with a series of missives between R'lyeh and the Leningrad Operational Center. These reveal that the initial assassination attempt was the result of poorly-planned meddling in human affairs; the final one explains how the manipulation of Yezhov and the sacrifice of a Lloigor agent had resulted in a violent program which would keep the secrets of the supernatural puppet masters safe for centuries. Behind the Mythos During the course of his investigations, Yezhov discovers a small statue in the apartment of the assassin which he describes as looking like " a bat-winged man with staring eyes and a beard of squidlike tentacles ." This is a clear nod to the statuette recovered during Inspector Legrasse 's 1907 raid of the Cthulhu Cult , and ties in with the R'lyeh communications which exposit the antagonist's motivations in "Red Star, Yellow Sign."

[3] Lloigor L83
Behind the Mythos During the course of his investigations, Yezhov discovers a small statue in the apartment of the assassin which he describes as looking like " a bat-winged man with staring eyes and a beard of squidlike tentacles ." This is a clear nod to the statuette recovered during Inspector Legrasse 's 1907 raid of the Cthulhu Cult , and ties in with the R'lyeh communications which exposit the antagonist's motivations in "Red Star, Yellow Sign." Although the entity encountered by Yezhov is named as a Lloigor, it bears no resemblance to the more commonly depicted members of that species, being described as having "vast eyes like glowing saucers, surrounded by a mass of squirming tentacles patterned in colours that shifted and shimmered," a much more generic Cthulhu Mythos description than its reptilian namesake. The Yellow Sign mentioned in the title refered to symbols etched on the statue found by Yezhov and imprinted on sewer walls by the Lloigor. Usually associated with the Great Old One Hastur , in this story the Sign was tied to Hastur's half-brother Cthulhu , the two entities being more commonly depicted as antagonistic in later Mythos stories. Trivia The assassination of Sergei Kirov was a real-world event which occurred in the Soviet Union in December 1934.

[4] Lloigor L89
Although the entity encountered by Yezhov is named as a Lloigor, it bears no resemblance to the more commonly depicted members of that species, being described as having "vast eyes like glowing saucers, surrounded by a mass of squirming tentacles patterned in colours that shifted and shimmered," a much more generic Cthulhu Mythos description than its reptilian namesake. Usually associated with the Great Old One Hastur , in this story the Sign was tied to Hastur's half-brother Cthulhu , the two entities being more commonly depicted as antagonistic in later Mythos stories. Trivia The assassination of Sergei Kirov was a real-world event which occurred in the Soviet Union in December 1934. The killing would cause the already-paranoid state leader Joseph Stalin to initiate the Great Purge, a political cleansing which would result in the deaths of hundreds of thousands.

--- Saucers from Yaddith.txt ---

[1] Nug L43
НАЗВАНИЕ: Saucers from Yaddith ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:27:49 СИМВОЛОВ: 836 Saucers from Yaddith Author Robert M. Price Language English Genre(s) Horror Science Fiction Publication Esoteric Order of Dagon APA Saucers from Yaddith " is a short story by Robert M. Price featuring Arwassa Overview In this story it is suggested that the Nug-Soth have visited Earth repeatedly from their homeworld of Yaddith to abduct humans and perform medical experiments upon the abductees. The experiments range from the swapping of a man's blood type from O to A to the swapping of eyes and hands to more nightmarish medical procedures. Obviously, this is a Mythos version of the Alien Abduction belief. "Saucers from Yaddith" was first published in the Esoteric Order of Dagon APA . It has since appeared in Etchings & Odysseys 5 (October 1984), The New Lovecraft Circle (1996), and Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008).

--- Servitor race.txt ---

[4] Zhar and Lloigor L253
As for their origins, many servitor races are believed to have been created, spawned, or sired by their masters. For instance, the Tcho-Tcho people are said to have been born from "seeds" left by Zhar and Lloigor, and have since been trying to free their progenitors from the subterranean chambers where the Elder Gods have trapped them ( AWD The Lair of the Star-Spawn "). The Miri Nigri were given life by Chaugnar Faugn , who made them from the flesh of Earth animals. Unlike most other races, the Miri Nigri have no mind of their own, and live only to serve their creator.

[5] Nug L317
Conversely, the Brothers of Chaugnar Faugn are more accurately described as dimensional extensions of Chaugnar, as opposed to individual beings ( CIRCLE The Horror from the Hills ). Similarly, the Fire Vampires are merely extensions of Fthaggua CIRCLE The Fire Vampires "). The Shoggoths, meanwhile, are a rather unique case, in that they were created by the Elder Things ( HPL At the Mountains of Madness ) but chose instead to venerate and serve Ubbo-Sathla EXP The Descent into the Abyss In " Dreams in the House of Weir ", by Lin Carter, the Dholes are explicitly called Shub-Niggurath 's "servitors", while the Nug-Soth are only identified as her "worshipers", possibly implying a distinction. Despite venerating the same deity, these two species are blood enemies.

The Book of Eibon identifies Nug as the "grandfather of all ghouls on the earth-plane" ( EXP The Descent into the Abyss "), but other sources claim that Nug never inhabited the Earth ( HPL Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft ), although it might still have visited it. This mysterious entity is mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft 's letter to James F. Morton as a descendant of Cthulhu which spawned Yogash the Ghoul. Yogash in turn is the ancestor of K'baa the Serpent and Ghoth the Burrower . The latter would have sired with a Roman noblewoman Viburnia the legendary ancestor of Lovecraft himself.

Meaning of the Shape Clithanus wrote that "the five points [mark] the directions of the earth and the secret place beyond the earth from which the things of Evil had first come" [ Depths online text )] . The "secret place" might be in the constellation Orion , where Rigel and Betelgeuse were the source of the Elder Gods (1) and their slaves such as Lloigor and Zhar , according to Dr. Fo-Lan Lair ]. Or it could be a reference to the constellation Taurus , home of the Hyades and source of Hastur Island Keeper ]. The star-stones' shape resembles the traditional pentagram that is much used in magic spells. Variants There are some instances of stones that resemble star-stones but have an overall different shape. Seneca Lapham had two ovoid-shaped grey stones, each small enough to affix to a bracelet or armband.

Competent scholars have traced, in a rough way, the advance or retrogression of racial groups in ethical and esthetic directions merely by studying and comparing their objects of worship and there does not exist a more fruitful science than idolography. "But occasionally our ethnologist encounters a nut that he cannot crack, a god or goddess so diabolical or grotesque or loathsome in conformation that it is impossible to link it associatively with even the most revolting of tribal retrogressions. It is a notorious fact that human races are less apt to advance than circle back on the course of evolution, and that idols and fetishes that were originally conceived in a comparatively noble spirit very often become, in the course of time, embodiments of the bestial and the obscene.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Stranger Crossings ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:29:29 СИМВОЛОВ: 1728 Stranger Crossings Author Adrian Chamberlin Country Wales Language English Genre(s) Cthulhu Mythos Publisher Screaming Dreams Publication Cthulhu Cymraeg Publication date October 2013 Stranger Crossings " is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Welsh author Adrian Chamberlin. It was published in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg by Screaming Dreams in October 2013. Synopsis When a dealer in antique books and artefacts identified only as "Taffy" is asked to evaluate a relic retrieved from a house clearance, he is unwittingly infected with the "spores of the Lloigor ." As he looks into his worsening condition and the provenance of the artefact, he comes to the realisation that it is a part of a group of objects necessary to conduct a ritual which will bring doom to mankind When he attempts to locate and destroy the piece, Taffy finds that the removals man has sold it to a folk band; further investigation suggests that they are in fact a cult who possess the other two objects necessary for the ritual, and have the necessary knowledge to conduct it.

--- Tcho-Tcho people.txt ---

[1] Zhar and Lloigor L73
Created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer The Tcho-Tcho people are a fictional species of hominids in the Cthulhu Mythos . They were originally created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story " The Lair of the Star-Spawn Background The Tcho-Tcho people are a group of tribes of near-human beings native to Asia. They can be found in Burma, The Anderman Isles, Tibet, and Malaysia. They are genetically from humans, but they are notably smaller, have livid red skin, and other marked physiological differences. Legends point to prehistoric genetic engineering of pre-human ancestors by the Great Old Ones Zhar and Lloigor . These legends purport they "grew from the 'seeds' of the Twin Obscenities". The Tcho-Tcho people are feared by other tribes and appear to be inimical to Mankind, while worshiping various deities including Han Chaugnar Faugn Rhan-Tegoth Hastur and his spawn. They appear to be the "corpse-eating cult of Leng" mentioned in the Necronomicon and have "lamas" as priests (cf. Elder Hierophant ). One source suggests that only the warrior caste are bred small. They might be related to the Men of Leng in the Dreamlands .


--- The Bell in the Tower.txt ---

[1] Nug L75
Williams has also found and purchased a copy of the Necronomicon It transpires that the Northam family has always dabbled in the occult as far back as Roman times. Lord Northam himself was drawn to the grimoires in the Northam estate's library which included the range of Mythos books. There he found a copy of the Necronomicon , many years prior. He also discovered a sealed tower on the estate. Entering it he discovered that the tower's belfry houses a giant silver bell. The bell was inscribed with " Nug-Soth " runes. Lord Northam discovered a forbidden ritual in connection with the ringing of this bell. The ritual, involving hallucinogenic drugs and the tolling of the bell summoned a procession of human figures on the fields below the tower, from all eras of mankind. Northam became addicted to viewing this procession and in the process addicted to the drugged ritual. Gradually and originally almost imperceptibly, less human figures began to join the procession during each ritual.

Well, he paid me off without a word at Hong Kong, and I went down the gangplank with Mike at my heels, feeling kind of queer and empty, though I wouldn't show it for nothing, and acted like I was glad to get off the old tub. But since I growed up, the Sea Girl's been the only home I knowed, and though I've left her from time to time to prowl around loose or to make a fight tour, I've always come back to her.

[1] Nug L43
I liked not what I saw and knew that even in mine astral form I might meet with untold dangers in such a place. Like a drifting spectre I passed over the desolate and much-cratered face of Pnath, seeking a certain Pit, named in suppressed legends as the Abyss of Noth, whereunto the cryptical whispers of dead Shahrajah had directed me. I lingered a moment upon the Precipice of Noth to gaze at the fearful spectacle outstretched in the shifting infra-red vapors below me. For there lay none other than the blighted Necropolis of Nug-Hathoth of which the ancient lore-masters record naught that is wholesome. I must needs take care to arrive no sooner than the fateful Hour of the Opening of the Under Burrows, the which I should know by the noxious Rising of the Black Wind which would bear up unto my ears the terrible gruntings of the Dholes as they issued forth in blind fumblings to commence their charnel feastings. I deemed it best to settle down upon the crest of the upthrust Tower of Narghan, and there to await the emergence of the eyeless slugs from their curiously asymmetrical burrows.

--- The Descent into the Abyss.txt ---

[1] Nug L117
Deep within the abyss, Haon-Dor hopes to locate the domain of Ubbo-Sathla , and retrieve the Elder Records : the stone tablets stolen from the Elder Gods Once inside the tunnels, Haon-Dor comes across Zushakon , one of the entities spawned by Ubbo-Sathla, and respectfully asks to be allowed passage while displaying the sigil known as the Elder Key . Later on, he enters a huge cavern, with alcoves gnawed into the stone wall. Inside each of these is a creature, which Haon-Dor recognizes as the "prototypes" of several races that serve the Great Old Ones Quumyagga of the Shantaks Nug of the Ghouls , etc. , each being the first of their respective kinds to have been created. To each of them, Haon-Dor asks for passage and shows the sigil. Leaving the Cavern of the Prototypes behind, Haon-Dor crosses a bridge over a colossal chasm and finds a luminous portal guarded by K'thugguol , the prototype of the Shoggoths . Unexpectedly, the Shoggoth allows Haon-Dor entrance even before the sorcerer has time to ask it.


--- The Doom of Enos Harker.txt ---

[1] Zhar and Lloigor L173
From them, Blaine learns more about the ancient deities, said to have been defeated by their enemies, the Elder Gods , who placed something called the Elder Sign to keep their foes imprisoned long before the evolution of mankind . The Great Old Ones ' servants, however, are still free to move about and do their masters' bidding. Said servants include the fish-like Deep Ones which serve Cthulhu, as well as the Tcho-Tchos who serve Zhar and Lloigor Above all, Harker is looking for someone to translate the R'lyehian language of the appropriately named R'lyeh Text , some portions of which are kept in the library at Miskatonic. Fortunately, a journalist who has investigated the circumstances of Bryant Hoskins' death reveals to the public that Hoskins had produced a translation of the R'lyeh Text , currently held in Miskatonic. On the next day, Blaine heads straight to the library to have a look at it. Completed version by Laurence J. Cornford The librarian, Dr. Cyrus Llanfer, refuses to allow the Hoskins manuscript to leave the university, but agrees to make a photostat copy for Dr. Harker.

[ Lair In his stories, Derleth does not explain why the Great Old Ones (3) rebelled. He has to work for hours on the simplest trick—and then he's liable to forget it. If he was a bonehead, I'd understand it. But he's brainy in other ways." --- The Key of Solomon the King Clavicula Salomonis (S.L. MacGregor Mathers) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).txt ---

[27] Nut L5277
The characters shown should be traced thereon. Thou shalt perfume them according to the rules of Art; and wrap them in silk cloth like the others. Figure 68 The staff Figure 69 The wand The Staff (see figure 68 ) should be of elderwood, or cane, or rosewood; and the Wand ( figure 69 ) of hazel or nut tree, in all cases the wood being virgin, that is of one year's growth only. They should each be cut from the tree at a single stroke, on the day of Mercury, at sunrise.


--- The Lair of the Star-Spawn.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L61
НАЗВАНИЕ: The Lair of the Star-Spawn ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:31:49 СИМВОЛОВ: 4513 The Lair of the Star-Spawn Author August Derleth and Mark Schorer Country United States Language English Genre(s) Horror short story Publication Weird Tales Publication date August 1932 WT "The Lair of the Star-Spawn" is a short story written by August Derleth and Mark Schorer on August 1932 and published in Weird Tales . It is notable as the first story to reference the Tcho-Tcho people and the entity Lloigor Synopsis Eric Marsh is part of a scientific expedition led by famed explorer and scholar Geoffrey Hawks to Burma, c. 1902, in search of the legendary city of Alaozar, to be found in the Lake of Dread on the Plateau of Sung . The natives are reluctant to provide guides, due to fear of the " Tcho-Tcho People " said to live there.

[2] Lloigor L93
As he watches, he is struck from behind and blacks out. He wakes up, bandaged, in a bed in Alaozor. He's greeted by Dr. Fo-Lan , a Chinese scientist who was thought to have died three years earlier. Instead Fo-Lan has been a slave of the Tcho-Tchos, forced to help them unleash an awful terror upon the world. Fo-Lan tells Marsh that the two of them can now thwart the Tcho Tchos' sinister plans. Fo-Lan leads him down a secret passage, where they watch the Tcho-Tchos bow down to their leader, the priest E-Poh ("he is seven thousand years old," says Fo-Lan), and the tentacled monster that lurks in the shadows, which Fo-Lan informs him is named Lloigor . Fo-Lan asks Marsh to watch his body while he astrally projects to get help. This goes off without a hitch. Once back in flesh, Fo-Lan informs him that he must convince E-Poh to open the gates to Zhar and Lloigor , at which time "the Star Warriors" can come and save them.

And on that day we will open the way to our friends from above, and join with our enemies in the final battle, the Armageddon that must forever decide the fate of the earth and the disposition of its people." Leo shifted uneasily in his chair. He had been made increasingly uncomfortable by the other’s speech. By now it was clear to him that his host was either a religious fanatic or a flying saucer nut, and that it was only a matter of time before he brought out his scriptures and his tracts. Suddenly Leo was very anxious to be gone. He glanced at his watch. "God, look at the time! It’s after two already. I’d better get going or we’ll neither of us get any sleep tonight." But the threat of Leo’s departure seemed to shock the old man into something closer to reality. "I guess you think I’m pretty crazy," he said in a more natural voice. "I can’t say I blame you.


--- The Necronomicon Gamebook_ Dagon.txt ---

[1] Nut L65
Riuscirai a impedire che il rito di Yule si compia, salvando l’umanità da un destino raccapricciante, o impazzirai prima? THE NECRONOMICON GAMEBOOK - DAGON is a literary adventure where you can personally experience the horrors narrated by HP Lovecraft in some of the most famous classic tales of the Cthulhu cycle: Dagon , Il rituale and Il segugio (in the volume you will also find a section dedicated to Terre del Sogno, with some suggestive extracts from Kadath ). The stories have been adapted with the utmost fidelity starting from the original text, so as to allow you an interactive immersion in the style of the master of the supernatural through a cross-over narration in which, armed with a nut and pencil, you will travel through the streets of Kingsport , you will confront each other with monstrous creatures, you will explore nightmarish territories and you will cross the border that divides dreams and reality. Will you be able to prevent Yule's ritual from happening, saving humanity from a gruesome fate, or you will go crazy first? Publishers description Design Team Written by: Valentino Sergi Artwork by: Alberto Dal Lago and Jacopo Schiavo Production staff: Valentino Sergi


--- The Night Sea-Maid Went Down.txt ---

[1] Nuit L123
After its initial appearance in The Caller of the Black , "The Night Sea-Maid Went Down" was included in Lumley's collection of Mythos short stories, Haggopian and Other Stories Subterranean Press , 2008). It was also reprinted in Sea-Cursed: Thirty Terrifying Tales of the Deep (Barnes & Noble Books, 1994), The Starry Wisdom: A Tribute to H. P. Lovecraft (Creation Books, 1995), and Brighton Shock! PS Publishing , 2010). A French translation appeared under the title "La nuit où la Sea-Maid fut engloutie," in a French edition of Lumley's stories, Compartiment terreur (Néo, 1989).

The story turned Lloigor August Derleth 's minor Great Old One , into an alien species of psychic vampires --a depiction that has influenced subsequent writers, including Robert Anton Wilson Alan Moore , and Grant Morrison Synopsis Wilson's story follows Paul Lang, a 72-year-old professor of English literature at the University of Virginia. Lang makes a breakthrough that allows him to decipher the Voynich Manuscript--a real-world tome written in an unknown script --and finds that it is the text of a book called the Necronomicon . (Urquart is a fictionalized version of "Colonel" James Churchward , a Devonshire engineer who concocted the lost continent of Mu Urquart tells Lang about the Lloigor, alien entities, probably from the Andromeda galaxy, that "existed as 'vortices' of power in their natural state." The Lloigor enslaved humanity on Mu before becoming weakened and retreating underground and beneath the oceans.

Their minds were a unity, not compartmentalised, like ours. There was no distinction in them between conscious, subconscious, and superconscious mind. There was no distinction in them between conscious, subconscious, and superconscious mind. So they saw things clearly all the time, without the possibility of averting the mind from the truth, or forgetting. Urquart compares them to "those suicidal romantics of the nineteenth century, steeped in gloom, convinced that life is a pit of misery, and accepting this as a basis for everyday life." The Lloigor are said to have retreated under the earth and sea, in order to concentrate their power in stones and rocks, whose normal metabolism they can reverse. This has enabled them to cling to the earth for many thousands of years. Occasionally, they accumulate enough energy to erupt once again into human life, and the results are whole cities destroyed.


--- The Sandwin Compact.txt ---

[1] Lloigor L79
He confides to Dave that he is convinced that whatever is making these sounds is speaking to Asa. Sometimes the sounds seem to come from the sea, other times from the sky, and occasionally from the underground. Additionally, Eldon has also heard music at night, which makes him dream of strange places. When he retires to bed, Dave himself experiences the same dreams and, on the next morning, the cousins hear Asa conversing with creatures with inhuman voices inside his room. Asa tells these visitors that he has "closed the passage" that would allow Cthulhu to reach him, and taken precautions against Ithaqua , but when the creatures speak the name Lloigor , the old man has no response. Dave recognises these names from certain books he has read at Miskatonic. Illustration by Hannes Bok Weird Tales When Dave and Eldon open the door, they see that Asa is alone, but the room is filled with vapour and there are pools of water on the floor. As he realises that his son and nephew have heard the conversation, Asa decides to tell them the truth.

[2] Lloigor L101
Generations ago, the Sandwins have made a compact with the Great Old Ones and their servitors , who have provided them with treasures and knowledge in exchange for an afterlife of servitude. If one were to open the graves of Asa's ancestors, they would find them empty, as each Sandwin has been seized upon death to live an "unnatural life" elsewhere. In order to spare Eldon of this same fate, Asa decided to break the contract. As a result, the creatures are now trying to take Asa before his time, and while he isn't afraid of Cthulhu or even Ithaqua (with whom Asa has traveled in the winds), he feels far less secure about how to avoid the wind elemental Lloigor. Several weeks pass by, during which Asa's physical appearance deteriorates, becoming increasingly frog-like and even shrinking. Eventually, Dave is forced to return to Arkham to resume his work, but is called back by Eldon one night when the star Arcturus is visible during the full moon, and the whippoorwills sing continually. Ambrose has left the house in fear.

[3] Lloigor L111
Eventually, Dave is forced to return to Arkham to resume his work, but is called back by Eldon one night when the star Arcturus is visible during the full moon, and the whippoorwills sing continually. Ambrose has left the house in fear. Outside, the night is windless, but inside, there is an inexplicable wind blowing through the whole interior, as well as an equally inexplicable "wall of air" that prevents Dave and Eldon from reaching Asa's room. Powerless to help the old man, the two are horrified to hear the same music from their dreams, accompanied by the sound of impossible footsteps and inhuman voices chanting in adoration of the god Lloigor. This cacophony culminates in a horrible scream, which both cousins recognise as Asa, at which point they both faint. When they regain consciousness, the house is back to normal, so they break the door open and enter the room, only to find Asa's empty clothes on his chair, as if his body had been sucked out of his clothes while he was wearing them. Behind the Mythos This story reveals that Miskatonic University has multiple librarians, including the narrator, Dave.
